title: Fit worse on purpose
hook: A curve hits every training dot. Why would you make it miss?

knows: that a too-flexible curve can overfit its training points
that held-out points check a model
doesNotKnow: the standard cure of penalising large coefficients (ridge)
that the cure makes the training fit worse

misconception: A model that fits its training data worse must be a worse model.
objective: The learner can explain that a penalty on coefficient size gives up some training fit for a calmer curve, that held-out error usually improves at a moderate penalty, and that too strong a penalty loses again.

claims.text: The toy fits a degree-7 polynomial to 8 training dots drawn from sin(0.8πx) plus noise (sd 0.3) at evenly spaced x in [-1, 1]; 40 held-out dots come from the same noisy curve. 'Miss' is the root-mean-square vertical distance from dots to curve.
claims.source: The lesson's own model in Demo.tsx (makeData, rms). Data set 1 is mulberry32 seed 1, the first seed, untuned; 'New data' steps through seeds 2, 3, ...

claims.text: Ridge chooses the curve that minimises the sum of squared misses plus λ times the sum of squared coefficients (the toy leaves the intercept unpenalised).
claims.source: Hastie, Tibshirani & Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., §3.4.1 (ridge regression, intercept not penalised). Implemented by fit() in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: With no penalty the degree-7 curve passes through all 8 training dots (miss 0); any penalty above 0 moves it off them, and the training miss never falls as λ grows.
claims.source: 8 points, 8 coefficients: the interpolating polynomial has zero training error. Ridge training error is non-decreasing in λ (standard result; the penalised solution trades residual for coefficient size). Checked in the toy: training miss non-decreasing across the 7 λ values in all seeds 1-500 (script reproducing Demo.tsx). Data set 1: 0, 0.084, 0.128, 0.177, 0.260, 0.363, 0.502.

claims.text: In 490 of 500 toy data sets some moderate penalty (the best of five, 0.0001 to 1) beat no penalty on the held-out dots; the strongest penalty (10) did worse than the best moderate one in all 500.
claims.source: Seeds 1-500 of the toy, computed in the reveal by the same makeData/fit/rms that draw the stage, and by a separate node script (builder's; the fact-checker should re-run independently). Data set 1 held-out miss: 0.444 at λ = 0, 0.377 at λ = 0.01, 0.725 at λ = 10. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Wording note from the checker: the 490 counts the best of five lambdas, so 'a moderate penalty' became 'some moderate penalty (the best of five)'. Numbers unchanged; re-set to unverified because the text changed.

claims.text: Push the penalty to 10 and the curve goes much flatter and usually loses again to no penalty on the held-out dots.
claims.source: Reveal paragraph 2. The 'loses again' part holds: lambda 10 is worse than the best moderate penalty in 500/500 and 10,000/10,000 further data sets, and beats no penalty in only 12%. 'Nearly flat' is loose: over seeds 1-200 the lambda 10 curve's range is a median 37% (16%-58%) of the training data's range, versus about 2.7 units for the unpenalised curve; it is strongly shrunk, not flat. Wording concern for demo-builder (e.g. 'goes much flatter'). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. DISPUTED 2026-10-13: Re-ran model: at penalty 10 the curve loses to no penalty in 441/500 seeds (88%), so 'loses again' needs 'usually'; and 'nearly flat' is loose (the curve is strongly shrunk, median about 37% of the training range per earlier check, not flat). Fix: 'goes much flatter and usually loses again'. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13: Was 'nearly flat and loses again' (disputed: loses in 441/500 seeds, 88%; curve is strongly shrunk, not flat). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-ran model.ts from Demo.tsx over seeds 1-500: lambda 10 held-out miss worse than no penalty in 441/500 (88%) so 'usually loses'; curve range at lambda 10 is a median 37% of training range (95% range 21%-54%), 'much flatter' fits.

recall.question: Model A fits its training data perfectly. Model B, trained with a penalty on complexity, misses some training points. Which is likely better on new data?
options: B, if the penalty is moderate
A, because it has zero training error
recall.why: A perfect training fit often bends to fit noise. A moderate penalty trades a little training accuracy for a calmer model that usually does better on held-out data; too strong a penalty underfits.
